finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> never enforces authorization. `require_allowed` is an alias of the boolean `is_allowed`, which returns True/False instead of aborting. The return value is discarded, so any caller can delete any file.
finding.source: Any HTTP client calling DELETE /files/<fid> with any or no X-Session-User-Verified header

trace.note: is_allowed only returns a bool and does not abort
The return value is ignored, so execution continues

finding.guards_checked: No decorator, no ensure_allowed call and no other check on the delete route. The rename route correctly uses ensure_allowed (views.py:26), which shows the delete route was meant to abort on denial.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: only the bare `require_allowed(...)` call (alias of bool-returning is_allowed), result discarded; no decorator or other check; before_request load_user only reads the header and does not enforce anything
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases bool-returning acl.py:4 `is_allowed` as `require_allowed`, views.py:18 discards its result, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any caller (unlike views.py:26 which uses the aborting `ensure_allowed` at acl.py:8-10).

finding.claim: The user identity is taken straight from a client-supplied request header (X-Session-User-Verified), with no session or signature validation. An attacker can impersonate any user, including the owner of a grant, and pass the ACL on the rename route.
finding.source: The X-Session-User-Verified request header, set by the attacker
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write") at views.py:26 and the rename at views.py:27, which trusts g.user

trace.note: g.user is set from the raw header
g.user is used as the ACL principal
The grants lookup is keyed by the spoofable user string

finding.guards_checked: No authentication layer, session store or signature check in the repo. The header name suggests an upstream proxy verifies it, but nothing in the code strips or validates it. If a trusted proxy overwrites the header and the app is not directly reachable, this is mitigated.

verdict.guard_found: none in the repo. The only control is ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), which aborts 403 correctly but is keyed on the spoofable g.user. A stripping proxy might exist outside the repo, but nothing here shows one.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user straight from request.headers with no validation, and views.py:26 passes it to ensure_allowed, which checks grants.get(user) at acl.py:5, so any anonymous client can send the header of a grant owner and pass the check; the only mitigation would be an upstream proxy that strips the header, which is not in the repo.

finding.claim: Missing or unknown file IDs raise an unhandled KeyError (HTTP 500). The existence check also runs before the authorization check, so the response lets callers distinguish existing IDs from non-existing ones. Related: if g.user is None, grants.get(None, []) is evaluated.

trace.note: Direct dict index with no 404 handling
Same pattern in the rename route

finding.guards_checked: No error handlers. This is low severity: it gives an ID oracle and a 500, not a bypass.

verdict.guard_found: none for the KeyError: no errorhandler or try/except, and STORE[fid] is indexed directly (views.py:17, 25). The ACL runs after the lookup (acl.py:8-10 for rename). Delete is worse: views.py:4 aliases the bool-returning is_allowed as require_allowed, and views.py:18 discards its result.
verdict.reason: views.py:17 and views.py:25 index STORE[fid] directly with no handler, so an unknown fid gives a 500 before any authz check, which acts as an existence oracle. The finding is accurate but low severity, and it misses a more serious bug at views.py:18, where the discarded return of require_allowed (alias of bool-returning is_allowed, views.py:4) lets any caller delete any file.
